concept.name: Averaging down
concept.definition: Adding to an existing long position as its price falls, which lowers the average cost per share and reduces the rebound needed to break even. It is a position-sizing practice rather than a complete strategy, most defensible within a valuation framework and strict risk limits.
concept.intuition: Buying 100 shares at $50 and 100 more at $40 puts the cost basis at $45, so the position needs only a 12.5% recovery from $40 instead of a 25% one - but the investor now owns twice as much of a falling asset.
concept.mechanics: Purchase additional shares at successively lower prices per a predetermined plan (fixed increments or valuation triggers). The new average cost is the share-weighted mean of purchase prices, and position size and portfolio concentration grow with each add.
concept.formula: Average cost = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i) over all purchases i.
concept.failure_modes: If the decline reflects deteriorating fundamentals rather than noise, averaging down concentrates the portfolio in a loser - the classic falling-knife path to outsized single-name losses.
concept.misconceptions: That a lower average cost means lower risk; the break-even math improves but total capital at risk rises with every add, and the practice is often used to avoid admitting a mistake rather than as a rational plan.
concept.example: 100 shares at $60 plus 100 more at $40 gives a $50 basis: the position needs only a 25% rise from $40 to profit instead of 50% - but $14,000 is now exposed to one stock.

citations.source: Investopedia, 'Average Down: Definition, How It Works, and Example'
citations.section: How the Average Down Strategy Works
